I played the decisions, then checked their consequences.

A fresh mobile-profile run entered through the real menu. I explored coronation, named and crowned a ruler, read the empty inheritance screen, chose the Granaries boon, selected a hero bringing neighbouring land, appointed a treasurer, chose Fortify, changed provincial focus, attempted a bribe and chose Salt Roads. The bribe failed and reduced trust; the report explicitly explained why. The realm later repelled its first invasion, with a named commander and 46 friendly losses in the inspected aftermath.

The grades below judge the current build’s design and usability. They deliberately separate system richness from demonstrated player enjoyment. Switch profiles to see where mobile comfort and desktop mastery change the weighting.
Editorial score, not a measured satisfaction rate. Decimal precision makes the weighting auditable; it does not imply certainty.
Combined is the equal average of the two weighted platform scores.
Rubric, weights, confidence and reasons for every grade

0–2 absent or obstructive; 3–4 weak; 5–6 functional but inconsistent; 7–8 strong; 9–10 exceptional and well supported. Product bands: below 40 D, 40–54 C−, 55–69 C, 70–79 B, 80–89 A−, 90–100 A. These are review conventions, not industry standards.

platform total = Σ(score out of 10 × weight) ÷ 10. Each platform’s weights sum to 100. Mobile weighs clarity, learning and pacing more heavily; desktop weighs strategy, economy, territory and combat more heavily. Combined averages the two totals. Confidence describes evidence strength, not a statistical interval.

Commercial fit, monetization quality, multiplayer and physical-device stability are not graded because this review does not establish them. Accessibility deductions reflect observed design constraints, not an unsupported claim of standards noncompliance.

Let mobile issue intentions such as “hold this crossing” or “escort this host”; preserve detailed routes on desktop.

Known enemy intent creates difficult decisions without demanding fast reading.

A player can understand the immediate problem, make a consequential choice, see its result and stop at a satisfying boundary. Low action count should reduce handling effort while preserving the need to choose.
This synthesis is an inference from the described designs and the local play review—not a market-wide user survey.

Experts should win by anticipating routes, managing commitments, exploiting interactions and responding to uncertain situations. More control should offer better plans, comparisons and execution—not compulsory maintenance clicks.
Vạn Thắng can retain one simulation and expose different planning surfaces. Shared rules make balance and teaching easier to reason about.

The target combines a rising base curve, ambition, rival pressure and bounded/lagged responses to defensive strength. The player-match factor has a free lead threshold and a cap; it does not cancel every power gain. Test the marginal benefit of a prepared wall or host, then expose a concise committed forecast.

Current prices respond to both the economic rate and excess stores. Older design notes describing income-only scaling are stale. Show how long a purchase takes to repay and whether a saved reserve is still meaningful; avoid reflexively deleting every anti-snowball rule.

Steward’s mean activity included roughly 21 focus changes, four governor postings, 14 manual claims and 128 sales. An action-heavy policy can win slightly more while being much less pleasant. Measure benefit per meaningful decision, not raw clicks.
The original shared-profile 64-run probe was retained only as a diagnostic. Fresh-profile reruns are the basis of the headline results. Evidence:
Nine proposals, refined through two critiques.

These loops are design reasoning informed by the current implementation and test evidence. They are not fabricated user-test rounds. Each ends with a smaller implementable direction and a criterion that could reject it.
01 · Keep combat readable as mastery rises
Add more speed and hide the counter guide in late waves, so experienced players must react and remember.

The current game already does this. Wave 13 enforces fast pace; later steps cap speech, raise enemy difficulty and hide assistance. Success can make the interface less accessible. Memorizing a ring is a different skill from choosing when to spend stamina.
Separate enemy competence, combat speed and reading assistance. Retain the player’s slow pace, explicit counter guide and optional automatic pause at a decision.
Unlimited stopping could remove time pressure for players who enjoy it. A globally slower battle could also make ordinary fights drag.

Ship independent settings: enemy difficulty, pace, readable intent, and pause-on-moment. Keep a clearly chosen timed challenge preset. Use stronger enemy plans and fewer safe responses to raise strategic difficulty; preserve assistance in normal runs.

At wave 20+, the selected slow speed and guide remain effective. In usability tests, at least 80% can explain the next enemy action before choosing a response. Treat that percentage as a target to test, not an existing result.
02 · A reign should sometimes end in triumph
Add a victory at wave 12, then end every run.
A mandatory cutoff would truncate a strong build. A fixed wave count also treats exploration, diplomacy and defence as the same achievement.
Offer a finite charter with a wave horizon and one thematic goal, followed by a choice to bank the result or continue.
Stacking several objectives can turn a relaxing phone run into a checklist. Banking too early may become the optimal progression farm.

Prototype one short charter: hold the capital through the first great invasion and preserve one chosen border. The initial candidate is the first four waves, tuned by observed wall-clock sessions. Award a complete ending; offer a second chapter or Endless. Later charters can emphasize trade or alliances. Normalize rewards by difficulty and meaningful milestones.

Candidate mobile chapter: 8–12 minutes including reading; desktop extended reign: 20–35 minutes. These are hypotheses. Keep only if players understand the goal and at least 70% of finishers want another chapter or a new build.
Remove most court cards and let autopilot handle the economy.
Cards are currently the main way many phone players exercise agency. Removing them would turn a grand strategy game into watching the simulation.
Queue routine advice in a compact court inbox; interrupt for danger, an expiring commitment or a genuinely new rule.
An inbox can become an invisible backlog. Too much batching can make all strategy happen in one exhausting menu.

Use the existing Aftermath → Court → Muster → Field structure. Present one strategic headline and up to three optional queued decisions. Pause for urgent, irreversible choices. Allow the player to pull any lane on demand. Let doctrine handle repeat maintenance under visible reserve budgets.

Target no more than two unsolicited full-screen decisions between ordinary waves after onboarding. Measure decision comprehension, ignored important events and actions per completed objective—not simply fewer taps.
04 · Make growth feel like an advantage
Remove all enemy adaptation and all price scaling.
The current game uses several bounded controllers, not a single unlimited rubber band. Removing everything could produce idle snowballs and trivial late-game purchases.
Publish the base wave, ambition, rival pressure and adaptive portion; lock a visible wave budget before the player finishes preparing.
A player may exploit the lock by hoarding strength until after the snapshot. Full formulas on a phone would be unreadable.

First instrument each contribution and run matched policy experiments. Prototype a muster snapshot with a bounded adaptation envelope. Count committed recruitment and construction when appropriate. Keep a short front forecast with a detail drill-down. Demand a measurable benefit from successful preparation before retuning all prices.

On the same scenario, a sensible defensive investment should improve losses, territory held or capital safety in a large majority of cases. Pre-register an 80% directional target and inspect exceptions. Compare outcomes as well as the displayed POWER.

Add dozens of new cards, units and building levels.
There are already 52 card definitions, 22 eligible for normal drafts and eight opening boons. More content may dilute the chance of forming a coherent plan and multiply balance work.
Audit the existing pool for three viable engines: fortified food/logistics, trading diplomacy, and mobile expansion. Give each a visible strength and a failure case.
Rigid engines could make drafts solved recipes; forced card bundles would reduce improvisation.

A food surplus might support a reserve host but face wage pressure; trade can fund defence but needs safe connections; expansion opens resources but stretches supply. Across 32–64 seeds and several competent policies, no starter engine should dominate every map. Players should name their build and its weakness after the second draft. Rework generic upgrades that cannot change a decision.

06 · One simulation, two comfortable ways to command
Give desktop players more compulsory micromanagement than mobile players.

Desktop already starts with Hands-on enabled, disabling autopilot and routine lane prompts. More chores are not automatically more depth, and platform defaults can conceal that this is a rules change.
Share the economic and combat rules. Let players choose Guided command or Hands-on command on either platform, with clear explanations and easy switching.
An expert workspace can overwhelm a phone; automation must not silently override explicit orders or make experts irrelevant.

Mobile uses intent presets, single-province drill-down and one urgent front at a time. Desktop adds pinned comparisons, stable shortcuts, routes, queues and optional multi-host selection. Both expose reserve budgets, order precedence and the same consequences. Prototype the command workspace with existing armies before adding units.

A desktop player can compare two fronts and queue a response in under 20 seconds after learning the controls. A mobile player can give an equivalent strategic intention in at most three major taps. Validate, do not assume, both targets.

07 · Make inheritance rewarding without obscuring skill
Merge Legacy, Dynasty and Cabinet into one universal currency.
A hard merge would discard distinct rewards and disrupt existing saves. Removing progression power overnight could make earned collections feel devalued.
Unify the explanation and end-of-run presentation while keeping the underlying stores. Distinguish permanent collection level, this-run stack and current-reign experience.
A prettier reward screen alone does not resolve grinding or fresh-profile disadvantage.

Use one inheritance summary: what was earned, what changed, and one optional next-run choice. Add a normalized challenge preset with clearly defined progression treatment. Prefer new options and sidegrades for future rewards; preserve existing ownership and test any balance migration separately.
At least 80% of testers can identify which of three rewards affects the next run, this run or collection completion. Compare new and progressed profiles with identical decision policies.

08 · Turn defeat into a useful next attempt
Add a detailed log explaining every multiplier after a loss.
There is already an aftermath and chronicle. A huge ledger may explain the engine while failing to help a disappointed player decide what to try next.
Show the decisive timeline: arrival, supply failure, formation exchange, reinforcement or capital loss. Offer one plausible alternative with an uncertainty label.
A counterfactual can be wrong when changing an order changes later random events. Automatic advice can sound falsely certain or blame the player.

Start with facts from the event log: “Relief arrived two seasons after contact.” Add a bounded comparison only where it can be simulated consistently. Let players replay a practice snapshot when feasible. Lead with the story and one learnable cause; keep the detailed ledger optional.
After a loss, at least 70% can name one specific adjustment for the next attempt. Verify every factual explanation against recorded events. Do not fabricate precise alternate win chances.
09 · Make Vietnamese strategy part of the rules
Build a full naval layer, historical campaign map and many new factions immediately.
That scope would compete with the current game’s clarity and balance problems. New movement, combat and economy layers would require extensive teaching and art.
Use existing formations, terrain, supply and character stories for a small historical scenario with a distinct tactical problem.
A famous battle becomes a trivia skin if the winning action is unchanged; a scripted historical win can remove agency.

Prototype one river-crossing or prepared-ground encounter. Telegraph its rule, allow more than one solution, and make a retreat/bait plan costly if mistimed. Keep historical framing separate from invented procedural outcomes. Expand only if this encounter changes players’ decisions and remains legible on a phone.
Players should describe the scenario’s terrain rule without opening a codex and use at least two successful approaches. Reuse existing systems before introducing a full navy.
Share the rules. Adapt the planning surface.

Use short evidence loops after each milestone. The thresholds below are proposed decision gates, not results from the current review. Avoid using a larger simulation score as the only shipping criterion.

begin with 8–12 people, split between mobile-first strategy players and experienced desktop strategy players. Treat this as qualitative discovery, not statistically representative market research. Observe a fresh profile without coaching.

time to the first consequential choice; time to the first understandable consequence; modal interruptions; missed costs; voluntary delegation; pause use; the reason for quitting. Candidate goals: first strategic choice within 60 seconds on the quick path, ≥80% correctly explain three of four representative choices, and ≥70% can name an adjustment after defeat. Revise the UI when people fail for the same reason.

32–64 world seeds × fresh/progressed profile × Guided/Hands-on × three competent plans. Use separate random streams for map, events and battle where possible. Report uncertainty and early/late outcomes; record the exact version, selected perks and cabinet levels.

charter completion, waves, land retained, friendly losses, capital safety, spendable reserves and decision count. Test one ablation at a time: income/wealth scaling, adaptation envelope, automation reserves and draft interactions. Do not reward deliberate refusal or stockpiling with a misleading “expert” label.
3. Tactical depth rather than memory alone

Compare competent counterplay, fixed formation, good retreat timing and commander delegation in the same battle scenarios. Vary army composition, terrain and supplies. Log reform exposure, stamina spent, moments answered and losses.

a readable opponent should remain challenging through its plan and tradeoffs. Preserve the slow setting and guide in ordinary late-game play. Ensure no formation or stance wins almost everywhere, and no single human-speed timing target is imposed on all players.

Test the four-wave short charter against the existing opening, with equal content quality. Measure wall-clock length including reading, completion/abandonment, whether the ending felt earned, and whether the player chooses another chapter or a different build.

evaluate the 8–12 minute mobile and 20–35 minute extended desktop hypotheses. Do not force a target duration by stripping the choices people enjoyed. Watch for repeat farming of the shortest reward path.

Use at least a lower-end Android phone/tablet and a representative iPhone, plus desktop keyboard/mouse. Test a sustained 20-minute run, dense combat, large text, repeated pause/resume and interruption while a choice is open.

a stable 30 FPS mode on the declared low-end target, with frame-time distribution, input latency, memory and thermal behavior recorded. Report p95 frame time against 33.3 ms rather than only average FPS. Test offline restore and pending rewards for duplication or loss. This review does not certify those budgets.
